Esau's pity was aroused by Jacob's bowing.
"To see your face is like seeing **the face of God**."

lessons.title: Joseph (1): The tunic, the dreams and the pit
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 37:15, 37:24 and 37:35 (read on Sefaria 11/11). 'Coat of many colours' is the King James rendering.

cards.title: The favorite son
cards.body: "Israel loved Joseph best of all his sons" and gave him **an ornamented tunic**. His brothers **hated him**, and then Joseph told them **his dreams** (37:3-7).

cards.q: "The pit was empty; there was no water in it" (37:24). According to Rashi, what was in it?
cards.why: Why add "no water" if it was empty? **Rashi**: no water, but **snakes and scorpions**.

cards.gloss: "an ornamented tunic" (37:3). The rare Hebrew word for its decoration has been translated many ways; the King James Bible made it the famous "coat of many colours."

cards.title: The man in the field
cards.body: On his way to his brothers, "a man came upon him wandering in the fields" (37:15). An ordinary stranger? **Rashi**: this was **the angel Gabriel**.

cards.gloss: "I am looking for my brothers" (37:16): said by the boy his brothers hate, on his way to find them.

cards.q: Who does Rashi say the "man" in the field was?
cards.why: **Gabriel**: a hidden messenger who keeps the story moving.
wrong_why: The brothers were already gone to Dothan.
That's the plain reading; Rashi brings the midrash.

cards.title: Empty, but not empty
cards.body: "The pit was **empty**; there was **no water** in it." Why say both? **Rashi**, from the Talmud: there was no water, but there were **snakes and scorpions**.

cards.title: He refused to be comforted
cards.body: Jacob mourns and **refuses to be comforted** (37:35). **Rashi**: no one can be comforted over someone **still alive** who is thought dead. It is decreed that the dead are slowly forgotten from the heart, but not the living. Joseph is alive.

cards.q: Why, in Rashi's reading, could Jacob not be comforted?
choices: He blamed himself for the tunic
cards.why: Comfort comes for **the dead**, who fade from the heart. Joseph was **alive**.
wrong_why: "All his sons and daughters sought to comfort him" (37:35).
Rashi gives a different reason.

points: A favorite son, **an ornamented tunic**, and dreams.
Rashi: the man in the field was **Gabriel**.
"**I am looking for my brothers.**"
The pit: no water, but **snakes and scorpions** (Rashi).
Jacob **refuses comfort**: Joseph is alive (Rashi 37:35).

lessons.title: Joseph (2): Adonai was with Joseph
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 39:3 (from Tanchuma) and Sotah 36b (cited by Rashi on 39:11), read on Sefaria 11/11.

cards.title: A slave in Egypt
cards.body: Sold by his brothers, Joseph becomes a slave in the house of Potiphar, an Egyptian official. Yet the Torah says, "Adonai was with Joseph" (39:2).

cards.q: Joseph's Egyptian master could tell that God was with him.
cards.why: "His master saw that Adonai was with him" (39:3). Rashi explains **how** he could see it.

cards.title: God's name in his mouth
cards.body: How could an Egyptian **see** that God was with Joseph? **Rashi**: the name of God was **always on his lips**. God's presence showed in how Joseph spoke and acted.

cards.q: According to Rashi, how did Potiphar see that God was with Joseph?
choices: God's name was always on Joseph's lips
Joseph told him about his dreams
cards.why: Not miracles: **Joseph's own speech** made God visible.
wrong_why: The Torah describes no miracles here.
The dreams aren't part of Rashi's answer.

cards.title: His father's face
cards.body: Potiphar's wife tries again and again to seduce Joseph. The Talmud: at the moment of greatest temptation, **his father's image appeared to him in the window**, and reminded him of **his place among his brothers**. Joseph fled.

cards.q: In Sotah 36b, what helped Joseph resist?
choices: His father's image appeared to him
cards.why: **Jacob's face**, and the memory of who Joseph was meant to be.
wrong_why: The Talmud's answer is more inward than that.
His own words (39:9) are about loyalty and sin, not fear.

cards.gloss: "Surely God can interpret!" (40:8). In prison, Joseph gives the credit away before he even hears the dreams.

cards.prompt: Joseph is a slave, then a prisoner, and still the Torah says God was with him. In this story, where does God's presence actually show up?

points: "**Adonai was with Joseph**," even as a slave.
Rashi: God's name was **always on his lips**.
Sotah 36b: **his father's face** in the window.
"**Surely God can interpret!**"

lessons.title: Joseph (3): Pharaoh's dreams
lessons.check_note: Torah text only, plus the custom of blessing children with Ephraim and Manasseh (Genesis 48:20).

cards.title: From prison to palace
cards.body: Pharaoh dreams of **seven fat cows and seven lean ones**, and no one can explain it. Joseph is brought **straight from prison** (41:1-15).

cards.q: Pharaoh says Joseph can interpret any dream. What does Joseph answer?
choices: "Not I! God will see to Pharaoh's welfare."
cards.why: "**Not I!**" (41:16). Again Joseph points away from himself.

cards.gloss: "Not I! God will see to Pharaoh's welfare" (41:16). Before he names God, Joseph answers in **a single Hebrew word**.

cards.title: Two names
cards.body: Joseph names his sons **Manasseh**, "God has made me forget completely my hardship," and **Ephraim**, "God has made me fertile in the land of my affliction" (41:51-52). Jacob later blesses them, and Jewish parents still bless their sons on Friday night to be like **Ephraim and Manasseh** (48:20).

cards.q: What does the name Ephraim say?
choices: God made me fertile in the land of my affliction
God made me forget my father's house
God made me ruler over Egypt
cards.why: **Ephraim**: fruitful **in the land of affliction** (41:52).
wrong_why: That's Manasseh's name.
Neither name says that.

cards.prompt: Ephraim: "fertile in the land of my affliction." Has anything grown for you in a hard place? It's fine to skip this one.

points: Joseph goes **from prison to Pharaoh**.
"**Not I!** God will see to Pharaoh's welfare."
**Manasseh** and **Ephraim**: forgetting hardship, and growing in it.
Children are still blessed **to be like Ephraim and Manasseh**.

lessons.title: Joseph (4): The brothers and Judah
lessons.check_note: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Repentance 2:1 (Touger translation on Sefaria), read 11/11. The observation that Genesis 37 records no plea from Joseph is from the text itself.

cards.title: Bowing to a stranger
cards.body: Famine drives Joseph's brothers to Egypt. They **bow** to the governor, as in Joseph's dream. Joseph recognizes them; **they do not recognize him** (42:6-8).

cards.q: When the brothers come to Egypt, they recognize Joseph.
cards.why: Joseph **recognized them**, but **they did not recognize him** (42:8).

cards.title: We looked on at his anguish
cards.body: Years later, the brothers say they **watched his anguish** and ignored him **as he pleaded** (42:21). Chapter 37 never mentions Joseph pleading. We hear his cry only now, **through their guilt**.

cards.q: What do we first learn in 42:21 that chapter 37 didn't tell us?
choices: Joseph pleaded with his brothers from the pit
cards.why: The plea is told **only in memory**, when the brothers' guilt surfaces.
wrong_why: There's no third dream.
Reuben wanted to save him (37:22).

cards.title: Complete teshuvah
cards.body: Long ago, **Judah** proposed selling Joseph (37:26-27). Now Joseph tests them with Benjamin, Rachel's other son, and Judah offers to **stay as a slave in his place** (44:33). **Rambam**: complete teshuvah is when you face **the same situation** again and choose differently, not out of fear or weakness.

cards.q: Why is Judah's offer a model of complete teshuvah, in Rambam's terms?
choices: He faces the same situation and chooses differently
cards.why: Same test, a brother at risk, and **this time he protects him**.
wrong_why: Rambam asks for more than words.
Gifts aren't the measure here.

points: The brothers **bow**, and don't recognize Joseph.
Joseph's plea from the pit is heard **only in their guilt** (42:21).
**Judah** offers himself for Benjamin.
Rambam: complete teshuvah is choosing differently **in the same situation**.

lessons.title: Joseph (5): I am Joseph
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Bereshit Rabbah 93:10 and Zohar, Miketz 11:182 (Soncino translation on Sefaria), read 11/11.

cards.title: He could no longer hold back
cards.body: Judah's plea breaks Joseph open. He sends everyone else out and says: "I am Joseph. Is my father still well?" (45:1-3).

cards.q: After "I am Joseph," what does Joseph ask first?
cards.why: His first question is about **his father** (45:3).

cards.title: The day of rebuke
cards.body: "His brothers could not answer him." **Abba Kohen Bardela**: woe to us on **the day of rebuke**. Joseph was the youngest, and his brothers **could not withstand his rebuke**. How much more, when **God** comes to rebuke each person **according to who they are**.

cards.q: What does Abba Kohen Bardela learn from the brothers' silence?
choices: If they couldn't face Joseph, how much harder to face God's judgment
cards.why: "I am Joseph" was rebuke enough. **The day of judgment** will be harder.
wrong_why: The midrash isn't about language.
The midrash reads the silence as shame, not mishearing.

cards.he: וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
cards.gloss: "although you intended me harm, God intended it for good" (50:20). After Jacob dies, the brothers fear revenge. Joseph answers: "Have no fear! Am I a substitute for God?"

cards.title: Not repaying evil
cards.body: The **Zohar** holds up "Joseph the righteous" as the model of one who **does not repay evil**: when his brothers fell into his hands, he told himself, "wait for the Lord, and he will save thee" (Proverbs 20:22).

cards.q: Why does the Zohar call Joseph "the righteous" here?
choices: He had his brothers in his power and did not repay evil
cards.why: Power over those who hurt him, and **he chose not to use it**.
wrong_why: The Zohar's point here is restraint, not dreams.
Power alone isn't righteousness; how he used it is.

cards.prompt: Joseph says God meant it for good, but it's Joseph who chooses to forgive. Where do you see God in that choice?

points: "**I am Joseph.** Is my father still well?"
Bereshit Rabbah 93:10: **the day of rebuke**.
"You intended me harm, **God intended it for good**."
Zohar: Joseph the righteous **did not repay evil**.
